learningObjective: Explain why FP16 and BF16 trade precision against dynamic range and identify a scenario that dictates the choice.

canonicalClaims.claim: BF16 provides FP32-like dynamic range (8-bit exponent) at the cost of 7-bit mantissa precision, versus FP16's 5-bit exponent / 10-bit mantissa; for DNN training where gradient dynamic range is critical, BF16 typically eliminates underflow/overflow issues that require loss scaling in FP16.
conditions: Hardware supports BF16 at competitive throughput.
The workload's precision requirement is compatible with 7-bit mantissa.
nonImplications: Does not imply BF16 always matches FP32 accuracy; mantissa precision can matter in some workloads.
Does not imply loss scaling is never required with BF16 — it is much less common but not universally absent.

misconceptions.claim: BF16 has more bits than FP16 and therefore takes more memory.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Both are 16-bit formats; total memory is identical.

misconceptions.claim: BF16 has the same exponent width as FP16; the two differ only in rounding.
misconceptions.whyWrong: BF16 has 8 exponent bits, FP16 has 5.

misconceptions.claim: BF16 is a fixed-point format so underflow is impossible.
misconceptions.whyWrong: BF16 is a floating-point format; underflow is possible but far less likely than FP16 due to the wider exponent range.

misconceptions.claim: Switching from FP16 to BF16 is always a Pareto improvement.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Reduced mantissa precision can cause small but real accuracy differences in some workloads (e.g., very small updates lost to rounding).

implementationFacts: Ampere Tensor Core: BF16 and FP16 have equal peak throughput.
performanceScenarios: LLaMA / GPT training typically uses BF16 for weights and activations.
Some vision workloads still prefer FP16 with loss scaling for precision reasons.
